newsitem.title: USA: Orange County, Calif., refiles suit against S&P.
newsitem.headline: Orange County, Calif., refiles suit against S&P.

text.p: Orange County, Calif., on Tuesday filed an amended lawsuit against rating agency Standard & Poor's for its alleged role in the county's financial crisis, county attorneys said.
Standard & Poor's is a division of McGraw-Hill Cos Inc.
The county amended its $500 million lawsuit against S&P after a U.S. District judge dismissed a portion of the county's complaint.
"We believe this (amended lawsuit) addresses the judge's concerns," county attorney Michael Swartz said.
Orange County filed for protection under Chapter 9 of the Federal Bankruptcy Code in December 1994 after sustaining investment losses of more than $1.6 billion.

Just before emerging from bankruptcy last June, the county sued S&P, alleging S&P's ratings assured the county that former Treasurer Robert Citron was "conservatively and safely" managing county funds.
S&P, which has denied any wrongdoing, asked the court to dismiss the county claims.

In a March ruling, U.S. District Judge Gary Taylor refused to dismiss the county's breach of contract claim against S&P. He agreed to dismiss the county's professional negligence cause of action, but told county attorneys they could refile.
The county's amended complaint, filed in District Court in Santa Ana, alleges professional malpractice as well as breach of contract, county attorneys said.
